items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then I left them and joined Jimmie Lunceford’s band.

ctx.x: . . . listened to a lot of different people.

Johnny Hodges, I just loved the way he phrased and played ballads. It was so hard for me. I would try to play things on the trumpet something like he played on the alto. There was another friend of mine, a fellow that I knew in Philadelphia, John Brown, who was an alto player who admired those fellows and was a very fine player. He became a very fine bebop player with Dizzy Gillespie’s band. He was a talented musician. He was someone who sort of took me under his wing. He was trying to teach me to play the…

they played it. I used to take – I used to listen – when I was playing these woodwind groups, I’d get some of their books, some of the textbooks, like a clarinet – a Klosé clarinet book. I’d try and play these things, and always trying to remember the way I heard the clarinet player, with that same concept. It helped me develop a lot of things.

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 1 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: I left that band and went with Jimmy Lunceford.

ctx.x: Oh, boy. Have you lived in New York most of your life?

I guess yes I have as a matter of fact, since 1947. I was born in Colwyn, Pennsylvania though. And I went into the Marine Corps for three years and when I came out I went back with Lionel Hampton and I stayed there a short time and I wasn’t very happy and I left that band and went with Jimmy Lunceford.
Were you able to play in the service?

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: I was with Jimmy Lunceford at the time of his death.

ctx.x: Wow. You’ve been on the forefront of a number of times of integrating things, in the studios in New York too?

Right, right, right. I was with Jimmy Lunceford at the time of his death. And when I came back I came back to New York and I went back to Philadelphia actually. And I stayed there for just a short time, then I joined Herbie Fields’ band. And he had had an integrated band on several occasions. It was a small group. But Frank Rosolino was in the band when I was there, and Rudy Cafaro was playing guitar, and Joe Gatto was playing piano. And we had really a nice group. Then after I left that band I went with Sam…

I wanted to ask you again, I brought it up the last time, but in watching you operate, you’ve been here for a few days on the campus and you seem to have a very well formed work ethic, as I’m going to call it. And you had told me about a few things that you believe are right in the way you operate your business and deal with other people. And I’m wondering, where did you get this work ethic? Was it something from your family?
